utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-74-PT, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Court Deputy. May I have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, Kenneth Scott for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Daryl Mundis for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'AOUST
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Josee D'Aoust for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll now turn to the Defence counsel and I will ask them to introduce themselves in the order they are seated. To start with Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Michael Karnavas for Dr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Suzana Tomanovic, co-counsel for Dr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Senka Nozica appearing for Bruno Stojic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Bozidar Kovacic for Mr. Slobodan Praljak and if I may introduce my co-counsel, Ms. Nika Pinter, who is not yet in this courtroom with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. I'm Nika Pinter, co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Vesna Alaburic appearing for Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Tomislav Jonjic appearing for the Accused Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and our legal assistant appearing for Mr. Berislav Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll greet everybody in the courtroom, the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, all the Defence counsel who have introduced themselves, and of course I also greet the court management staff, to start with Madam Court Deputy, the legal officer, the usher, the court reporter, and the interpreters in the booths who are going to help us today. In this hearing, which is going to take us, I hope, until quarter to two. We have a very full agenda for this Status Conference. I believe you have received this agenda, and I wish to add another item to the agenda today, a very essential one. I will mention it to you later on. You were aware of the agenda which was as follows: We have the pending motions; item 2, the state of health of the accused; item 2, the time the Prosecution will need for the presentation of evidence and possibly the issue of Rule 98 bis; fourth, the time that will be taken for cross-examination by the Defence; item 5, the issue of the admissibility of the exhibits or evidence; item 6, admissibility of video exhibits; 8, the testimony of expert witnesses; 8, opening statements by the accused and the time they will be given. There was a motion filed by the accused Praljak. Item 9, the issue raised by Mr. Praljak who was asking to be allowed to put questions to the Trial Chamber; item 10, sort of a progress report by the Prosecution as to the evidence sheet. Then we will have two items in private session. No need to speak about it now. And possibly miscellaneous. Of course, you know the next Status Conference will be held on the 12th of April. Before we move to the agenda itself, I wish to greet the two new lawyers. This is the first time I'm meeting them. Mr. Kovacevic, and Ms. Pinter who were appointed by the registrar following a decision by the Trial Chamber so that the accused Praljak may be represented. I also learned from the Registrar that Mrs. Nozica will also be assisted by Mr. Peter Murphy to defend Bruno Stojic. We still have accused with only one counsel. I informed the Registrar that it would really be good for them to have co-counsel. You never know. It may happen that a counsel falls ill, has the flu, falls from his bicycle, falls ill for a couple of days. It is therefore necessary for him or her to be replaced. You never know. Or slip on a piece of banana skin. So you have to be at least two people in a team. And I want to convey to you a piece of information dating from yesterday afternoon. I know that you carefully following everything that happens in the life of this Tribunal. The Security Council a Resolution, Resolution 1660, which creates a Reserve Judge. The Reserve Judge that was created by the Security Council had to be translated into the Rules. Mr. Karnavas participates in the work of the Rules Committee as representing the Association Of Defence Counsel. The Judges met yesterday, and we have amended Rule 15 bis. We now have a new Rule 15 ter. So in a nutshell, it will be four Judges sitting in this case. There will be a permanent Judge, myself, two Ad Litem Judges. So this will be the Prlic Bench, as it were. And we will have an Ad Litem Judge, a Reserve Judge to complement the Bench. But pursuant to Rule 15 ter (ii), the Reserve Judge will be present at all hearings, of course, will be allowed, if need be, through the Presiding Judge to put questions to the witness who will be testifying. However, the Reserve Judge will not take part in the deliberations reading to a vote. What is the use of the Reserve Judge? I ever were to pass away, me or another Judge or for whatever reason, then the time proceedings will continue, and the Reserve Judge, who will have been there from the very beginning, can then step in without any problem. There is another possibility provided for in the Rules, which is the possibility to call upon a Substitute Judge. This happened in the Milosevic trial. You remember that Judge May had to resign for health reasons, and he was replaced by Judge Bonomy. But the procedure of the Substitute Judge makes it necessary to have the consent of the accused whilst with the Reserve Judge it's sort of automatic. He's on standby, as it were, and if need be he can be asked to take part. There is no need to ask for the consent of the accused because the Reserve Judge will be present at all the hearings from the beginning of the trial. So the Rules were amended yesterday, and very soon you all will receive an amended version thereof. I want to thank all who contributed to the amendment so that this possibility is now on board. Furthermore, I'd like to move now to the item of pending motions. In this respect, as you know, three decisions were taken by the Trial Chamber since our latest Status Conference. There was one on the 17th of February, 2006. The Prosecution had filed a motion for the admission of UNPROFOR documents from the Spanish Battalion. There was one dated 14th of March, 2006, for judicial notice of facts agreed in other cases before this Tribunal, and you know that we took judicial notice of 88 facts. However, the facts might be opposed by the Defence during the trial pursuant to Rule 94(B) of the Rules. The decision taken on the 14th of March, 2006 denying a motion filed confidentially by Prlic regarding the striking of witness statements. As to pending motions, each time I wonder, because a lot of motions are supposed to be confidential. But that is also to be taken with a question mark. There was a confidential motion by the Praljak and Prlic Defence dated 25th and 26th of July 2005 regarding a request for production of documents addressed to a state. So I turn to Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Kovacic. Did the state answer, or are you still on standby?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as I understand, the state has been cooperating to some extent, and we are continuing to -- to work with the state to get necessary documents. That's the best I can say at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my position is about the same, and I have to admit you caught me a little bit off the guard, but at that time we -- we felt that we have to -- to ask Court's assistance, because the reactions of the government were extremely slow and some materials were not accessible simply without some additional pushing from this side, and that was the reason. And I may say that after that, the government did actually prove the delivery and some processes were much faster even though it might have been much better, because some materials we are receiving up to this day which normally might have been done year earlier. But it is not the wish of the government, so cannot ask this Court to press the government because it is not their wish. It is simply their inability to cope with administrative matters. So it's like asking you to change the weather. Thank you so much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood that I did not mention the state as such because this is a motion filed confidentially, so I'll speak in general terms. From what I understand from you, I can conclude that you received some documents at the level where you are. You feel that you should have received more. I don't know whether you want the Chamber to intervene efficiently. If you do so wish, you can do it now. You can do it later when the trial begins. You can file a motion with a very precise request for specific documents. We can then issue an order for the production of those documents to the said state. But the experience I have gained shows me that as a rule, states or institutions faced with such a situation tell us, "There's no problem. We just wanted to know exactly which documents you were requesting." So in your future motion, you will have to specify the documents you needed. It will then be much easier for the Trial Chamber to turn to the state for full cooperation otherwise, they can always tell me it wasn't specific enough, they didn't tell me. So you got me, you got my message. No oral decision today on these two pending motions. My conclusion is that as things stand the motion was met in part, but there's still a missing part which can be settled once the trial has started. We also had motions pursuant to 92 bis, (A), B), C and D. A decision will be rendered within the next 48 hours. The decision or the draft decision is being circulated among the Judges, and very soon you will have a decision. I also had a request dated 27th of December 2005 for the Defence to specify whether they're going to invoke a defence of alibi. There again, a decision will be issued soon. It was pursuant to Rule 67(A)(i). We also had a confidential request or application filed by the accused Prlic on the 7th of March as to the date of opening of trial. Recently on the 23rd of February, I think I settled the problem by issuing an order. This application is therefore moot. There is another motion filed by the accused Praljak on the 13th of March with an addendum dated 16th of March for leave to make an opening statement further to Rule 84 bis. Of course, the Trial Chamber will support the idea. The only issue is how much time will be made available, because the accused Praljak is asking for six hours. That would be fine if he were alone, but I'm not sure that the other five accused will also want to make opening statements. So we'll see in due course. If each and every accused wants to make an opening statement, we will have to strike a balance. If Mr. Praljak is the only one to wish to do so, he might be given anything from four to six hours. All this will be decided upon in due time. We had several other motions relating to the translation of documents. We have one from the Prosecution dated 24th of January, 2006, for the Chamber to tackle the issue of translation and asking for a deadline of the 6th of February for documents related to Rule 66 and 68. Now, accused Praljak, as a lawyer speaking English, so there's no problem any more. We were also seized of various filings by the accused Praljak who was not represented by a lawyer, and he also wanted documents to be translated. Inasmuch as it now has two lawyers, this motion is also moot. We had a motion by the Prosecution dated 2 December 2005, related to the order of 30th of November, 2005, for a paper -- paper copies of the documents, and we were told that by the accused Praljak that he was pleased with the electronic system. So this is also moot. So these were three technical motions. We will have a written decision soon joining them all and specifying that they are now moot. Other pending motions. On the 17th of February, the Prosecution had asked for leave to file a reply to the -- or a response to the reply by accused Praljak regarding the filings of the Prosecution dated 30th of January, 2006, related to the order of 24th of January, 2006. The response and the leave for reply are denied because there was no need to have a response. There was no need, therefore, to continue to process this issue. On the 22nd of February, the Prosecution had asked for leave to file a reply to the Defence pre-trial briefs. Thereafter, the Petkovic Defence filed a leave to respond including the reply. I remind you of the fact that the Defence pre-trial brief pursuing -- pursuant to Rule 65 ter (F) is not a motion which calls for a reply. The system is very simple indeed. The Prosecution drafts and files a pre-trial brief. The Defence is informed of it, and it will reply by answering and also presenting its views. But there must be an end to something, because otherwise it will be a never-ending process. In this case, I believe that the Trial Chamber has received the Prosecution pre-trial brief and the briefs filed by the six accused pursuant to Rule 65 ter (F). There's list the issue of disclosure of exhibits. I hope this is an ongoing process under Rule 66(A)(i), 66 (A)(ii) and also Rule 68. Should there be any problems remaining until the beginning of the trial, I do urge the Defence to get in touch with the Prosecution in order to settle them unless the problem is such that you need to tell me so. Failing that, I now move to the very core of this hearing. Only the 26th of March, 2004, the Security Council adopted a Resolution, Resolution 1534. In the said Resolution which also reminded Resolution 1503, the Security Council said the following, and I'm going to say is slowly so that the Prosecution can listen carefully, because what I'm about to say basically has to do with the Prosecution. This is what the Security Council was saying: "The ICTY is requested to take all necessary measures within their jurisdiction to finalise investigations by the end of 2004, to complete all trial proceedings by the end of 2008, and also to complete the Tribunal's work in 2010." Therefore, the Security Council requested that the Prosecutor and the President of the Tribunal go to New York every six months in order to take stock of the steps that have been taken in order to complete the trials by 2008. On this basis, we are now today in March 2006. There is the obligation, the urgent obligation given by the Security Council to complete all trials by 2008. We have the indictment. We have the pre-trial brief. We have the witness sheet or chart. The exhibit lists. Together with the rest of my team, I endeavoured to assess the time that the Prosecution will need in order to present their case. This work took some time, because we had to add up hours, taking into account the estimated number of witnesses, and we ended up with the following figures: If we were to go by the Prosecution's intentions, we might have a trial that would last three years, two weeks, and four days, because you would need for your examinations in chief 804, same time for the Defence, 804. Then re-examination, 10 per cent, so 80. Questions by the Judges, 10 per cent as well, some 92 bis witnesses who might come for cross-examination. All this would give 2.123 hours. In other words, three years, two weeks, and four days. Last time I saw you, I told you that as far as I could see it personally, I thought the trial would take four years. In the calculation I've just made, I mentioned three years. Then we would have to grant the Defence another three years. So the trial, all in all would last six years, which is impossible. So if we take it from there everything now becomes clear. I'm turning to the three representatives of the Prosecution. We all have, the Prosecution, the counsels, and the Bench, we are under the obligation to finish in 2008. I would like someone to tell me, and I would like Madam Carla Del Ponte to come and explain things to us on the 12th of April, the next Status Conference, what she intends to do, because how can we go to New York and say that we have taken the necessary measures to finish by 2008 when we adopt a system whereby the Prosecution has three years to present its case? So this raises a very serious problem. The Prosecution needs to consider this. Not all three of you, because you're -- the senior Prosecutor was in Brussels and Belgrade, and he is a person who has to manage this case. This is not something that is totally new in this Tribunal. The -- Slobodan Milosevic, which was a flagship case in this Tribunal, this case had also been addressed and the time issues had been addressed. Let me remind you that there were three indictments, and at the time Judge May had intervened on the 10th of April, 2002. Let me refer you back to the transcript of the hearing. Page 2782 to 27885. Judge May had explained that a trial must be fair. There should be fairness on both sides, fairness for the Prosecution and fairness for the Defence, and that it was also important to bear in mind the time spent on the case. Judge May said, "The longer case, the more difficult the judgement will be." This, of course, is just a matter of common sense. Judge May had indicated that it was for the Prosecutor to present its case. The Prosecutor should be granted the possibility to do this. It was for the Prosecution to carry the burden of the proof, and I entirely share this view. But Judge May was very much aware of the problem and had at the time stipulated that the Milosevic trial would take 14 months. You all know that after this oral decision was rendered on the 10th of May, 2003, a new oral decision was made thereby addressing the issue for yet another time. The Prosecution wanted to add a greater number of witnesses, and the Prosecution had been asked to speed things up. At that time, the Prosecution was granted an extra 120 days to be able to call further witnesses to testify. So this is an example we have, the Milosevic case. But I have also another example that comes to mind, and that is the Nuremberg trial. In the Nuremberg trial there were a greater number of accused. The events had taken place on a global level. There had been millions of victims. At the Nuremberg trial it was completed in less than a year. Based on these facts, what are we to do? As a Pre-Trial Judge, but I'm also the Judge presiding over this Chamber, I turn to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence where I do find a solution. Article 90(F), which I shall read out slowly: "The Trial Chamber shall exercise control over the mode and order of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence as to make the interrogation and presentation of evidence effective for the ascertainment of the truth and avoid needless consumption of time." So the Judge therefore has to make sure there is no needless consumption of time. This is why I have asked the Prosecution to move quickly so that I can have this chart to understand which witnesses will be called, what the allegations are, and what the exhibits are so that I get the overall picture and that I understand what it is the Prosecution is presenting in this case. But I can also -- I may also feel that some witnesses are not particularly useful. As you know, it is for the Chamber to determine the list of witnesses. So we could well say out of these 400 witnesses, 200 will not come to call to testify. That is a possibility. I come from a culture where we don't impose things. I Try to come to an agreement and find a solution with parties who are able to work together and who consider all of this. Between now and the 12th of April, you will have time to reflect on all of this. But in the meantime, let me do my sums. So please pick up your pens, and you can tick on your pieces of paper the following items I'm about to list out. If according to the Resolution of the Security Council we are to finish this trial by 2008, which means that at that time the Prosecution will have one year to present its case, the Defence overall will also have one year to present its case. It's one year plus one year. That's two years. That leads us on to the year 2008 where we comply with the Security Council Resolution. There are 52 weeks in one year. Yes, you would like the floor?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I consider it my obligation to say this with respect to this matter. The political decision of the Security Council is undoubtedly of great importance for decision making as to the method of work in this Tribunal and its work organisation, and I consider, however, that a political decision by the Security Council cannot influence the organisation of the way in which this courtroom works, because when we come into court with a trial and legal proceedings undertaken, I think that all the parties in this courtroom must be tried fairly and justly. If we cannot ensure the conditions necessary for a just and fair trial in view of some political decision which sets a time limit on us, then I consider that we are faced with a serious dilemma as to what to do. I consider it my obligation to say my views on the matter and my stand, and in conclusion I'm going to say why I feel this need and duty to state my views and position. I consider that it is our primary task to ensure a fair and just trial. I also consider that the indictment and Prosecution must have sufficient time to call all the witnesses it deems necessary and, of course, it is up to the Trial Chamber and the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber to assess which exhibits are necessary and which proof is necessary to establish the facts that are considered to be relevant in this trial and legal proceedings. I also consider that the six accused in this trial cannot be considered just one group, that is say one subject for them altogether at their disposal as much time as the Prosecution has been granted. I think that these are six individuals who ultimately can have different defence concepts and that each of them has the right to defend himself with -- in full capacity, as if he were the sole accused in this trial, in these proceedings. That is why I consider that the minimum time to be seen and provided for a trial and the time accorded to the Defence is six times the amount of time necessary for the Prosecution. If we were to compare these trials these legal proceedings with all the other trials held at this Tribunal up until the present day, we will establish that we have the largest number of accused here, accumulatively the largest number of accused, the broadest geographical terrain covered, and the longest period of time concerned. Now, to expect such a complex trial, which we are calling a megatrial in this courtroom, should be completed by the end of 2008 I consider to be absolutely unrealistic, and I think that not a single trial, even a very small trial compared to our own trial has not been completed within such a short time span. Now, if decision-making on the methods of work in this courtroom be determined by a political decision taken by the Security Council that the trials must be over by the end of 2008, I consider that we won't be able to ensure a fair and just trial. And faced in a situation of this kind, I personally do not consider that I can do my job in the proper fashion, that I can defend my client in the proper fashion. And if work in this case and trial is conceived along those lines, I will be forced to table a request to relieve me of my duties, because I cannot take this responsibility on myself, on my shoulders, under these time constraints and time pressure. So that is the reason for which I have taken the floor. Now, the question remains, what can we do faced with a situation like that? I think there are two possible solutions. One solution is the following: If we assess that the political decision by the Security Council --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you. I'll give you the floor again. This, of course, you were turning to those people who were in the Security Council responsible for this. It is important to address these matters, of course, but this can be managed by providing a series of solutions. Before you took the floor, I was going to look into these solutions, and I will give you the floor again afterwards. As I was saying, I was asking the Prosecution to pick up its pen and paper to do the following sums: Now, if we reckon there is a year. There are 52 weeks in a year. If we take away the UN holidays, the winter/summer recess, and perhaps a few technical difficulties, we can, I think, work from 40 weeks. If we reckon we have five days' hearing a week, we have 200 hearing days per annum, which means that the Prosecution case could be presented in the space of 200 days. If a hearing starts at 9.00 and finishes at quarter to two, as you know from experience, we basically only have three to three and a half hours, because sometimes we have problems pertaining to the exhibits being tendered and a number of other problems. So basically examination-in-chief lasts three hours. So three hours multiplied by 200. That totals 600 hours, which means that if we are talking about one year in which the Prosecution would be presenting its case, we would have all in all 600 hours, all included. In other words, the time allotted to the Prosecution and the time allotted to the Defence for its cross-examination. The Prosecution would have a credit of 600 hours. The Prosecution should feel free to break down this time -- this time whichever way it feels best. But this -- as regards this breakdown, the Judge also have a say in the matter, because Judges need to make sure that no time is wasted, and we have two objectives in mind. A, the interests of justice, and the ascertainment of the truth. So these objectives, of course, take into account the indictment. We have three major areas in this indictment, the joint criminal enterprise, individual criminal spot of all the accused, and the facts, the facts which bring together a number of municipalities. These are the three main parts of the presentation of the case. From a personal standpoint, let me say that facts are important, of course, because facts need to be established. There are a great number of facts, as you know. There are huge facts. No later than yesterday, I looked into those facts that related to Prozor, where in the annex we find more than 175 items that need to be established according to the Prosecution. If I turn to these 160 items -- 175 items, I found 122 which each require a witness testimony to establish the truth of the fact which is mentioned. So all of this takes time. This is something we are all able to understand. According to the filings submitted by the Prosecution and looking into all the annexes that cover all these municipalities, in the tradition of this Tribunal, this could take a great deal of time. The facts have to be mentioned, of course. This is just a suggestion I'm making. Out of these 600 hours, I feel that one-third of the time could be dedicated to facts. In other words, 200 hours. If you divide this by the 12 municipalities and prisons, let me take the case of Gornji Vakuf, for instance, the Prosecution would have 20 to 30 hours to present the Gornji Vakuf facts. Now, with the remaining 400 hours, as I told you a while ago there are two very other important points, the joint criminal enterprise, which require evidence, and the individual criminal spot of each accused which needs to be proven by the Prosecution. This could also -- time could also be broken down in a particular way. A hundred hours dedicated to joint criminal enterprise and 300 hours for individual criminal responsibility. If I divide this time by the six accused there would be 50 hours that could be dedicated to each accused. This is just a cue I'm giving you. The Prosecution, of course, has to decide what it is it wants to do, but this does raise a very particular issue. And I feel it's my responsibility to talk about it. I have -- I listened very carefully to what was said about having a fair trial, and when there is a charge, the Defence of course needs to be able to provide its viewpoint during the cross-examination and by preparing its Defence strategy. There has to be equality of arms, of course, and a fair trial. But if we turn to cases that have been tried or could have been tried, like the Milosevic case, nothing is impossible, because the Prosecution can narrow the indictment. At any time the Prosecution can seize the Chamber with a view to amending the indictment. If you were in the navy, you say you can cut in the sail or reduce the sail. So this is a technical solution for those who like to sail. I know we have a naval officer in the room. So this is a possibility. By reducing the sail, you are able to fit it in the time that is being allotted to you. Another solution would be revolutionary in this Tribunal, but as far as I'm concerned would not be a particular problem. And the Rules of Procedure and Evidence provides for it, but as I said, this would be really revolutionary. The solution would be the following: The Prosecution could call its witnesses, but the examination-in-chief of the witnesses would start off by questions from the Bench so that what is essential is addressed straight away. After the questions by the Bench, the Prosecution then leads the evidence on the witness and then the Defence cross-examines the witness. So after those questions put by the Bench of course, we would focus on what is essential. This is a way of gaining a lot of time. Experience has demonstrated that when a witness testifies for an entire day, 15 or 20 minutes are really useful but the rest of the time isn't really useful. All you need to do is refer back to the judgements and testimony. This would be one way of doing things, but as I say, this would be so revolutionary that I -- this is only a suggestion I'm making. Unless, of course, everybody were to agree to this. And I would start off by asking questions or putting questions to the witness. I don't think the Prosecution has any intention of going along with this. Another solution which would be a far simpler solution would be the following. When a witness is called to testify, the Prosecution could focus on the core of the testimony and avoid asking questions which might be interesting from an intellectual standpoint, but as far as the case is concerned are not so useful, perhaps. Let me give you an example. Let's imagine we have a Witness X who has been a victim in a municipality. Let's call it Y. Are the following facts: This woman has been brought from her home, she is put in a camp, a detention camp, her house is burnt down, her property is looted, and in this camp she would have been abused. So the witness comes and comes called to testify. You know that there are a number of witnesses that fit this picture. So what is important here? It is important to understand whether what the witness is saying is true, whether this person has been beaten up, whether her house has been destroyed, and whether her property has been looted. So a whole series of questions can be put to her, and this deals with the heart of the matter. And if you put the questions cleverly, the witness can then say or talk about what has happened to her. This can last no more than 25 to 30 minutes. The question can be settled in a very short space of time. If the Prosecution deals with this in an efficient way, we can then hear three to four witnesses during a hearing, which is a considerable way of gaining time. We then focus the questions on the heart of the matter. In other words, what -- what the person has studied, what her status is and how many family members she has. This could be very interesting. But as far as the indictment is concerned, as far as the alleged facts are concerned, this is perhaps not so useful. However, it is most important that she describes what happened to her and who did what to her. So by focusing on the questions in this way, we can gain a lot of time. But this is for you to decide. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence provide for this possibility. I can intervene and say, "Please don't ask this question," but I think it's better when professionals deal with this directly. I think it's better to understand how it is -- it's better to understand how it's best to ask questions rather than having the Judges turn round and say no, you wasn't put the question properly and then everybody wastes their time. So this is just a suggestion I'm making. I would like you to think about this. I think Madam Carla Del Ponte in person is responsible for all of this here, because I don't think this -- I don't -- it's -- this case cannot last six years. Technically speaking, it cannot, but given the number of exhibits, the number of witnesses, the way the Chambers work, it could, in all likelihood last six years. But we cannot -- we do not have this sort of time. On several occasions the Security Council has indicated that if Ad Litem Judges have been appointed, that was the whole purpose of it. If there's -- a standby Judge has been appointed that was the whole purpose was to speed up the process. If we have drafted an 11 bis Rule, the whole purpose of it was to be able to refer some cases back to domestic jurisdictions and only try before this Tribunal the most important cases. So the Security Council really wishes this Tribunal to finish its cases since this -- the Tribunal will not go on forever. This is why as of 2004 onwards, new investigations have not been opened. So it's all very well to have a fair trial. Yes, of course you're quite right, and what you've said is something noted and I will hand it over to the president of this Tribunal, but all will depend on how the Prosecution will present its case. From a technical point of view, if we look into the number of witnesses, the number of exhibits, the number of municipalities and very complex issues at stake, the indictment and the way the indictment is currently drafted, I think it seems totally impossible to finish this case before two years, the two years are up. And if we are able to finish this case in two years, this means that a lot of effort and input will be made by all and everyone a change of mindset also. I want to address this issue with you to make sure that all the parties present were advised of this. If at this stage the Prosecution would like to say something, I'll be very willing to give them the floor, but I believe that it is for Madam Carla Del Ponte to advise the Chamber of her intentions. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and may it please the Court, I will certainly convey your invitation to Madam Del Ponte, and I'm sure that a much further response or more extensive response can be provided to you in the future. I will share with you in the next few minutes a preliminary or provisional response of some of our thoughts on the questions that the Chamber has raised. First of all, the Security Council Resolution of course is not directed to the Office of the Prosecutor by itself. The Security Council Resolution is directed to the ICTY as a whole. If the ICTY fails as an institution to proceed efficiently, there can be an entire host of reasons why that can be the case without any fault of the Office of the Prosecutor. If the ICTY insists on going forward on the most conservative common law approaches and is not innovative in what it does, then indeed the institution may fail, and that would not be due to any fault of the Prosecution. This Prosecution team for the last two years has done everything within its power to move this case as efficiently as possible. We've used every available tool, some in traditional ways and some in ways that we've proposed as to be more creative in how we might move this case forward. We over a year -- about a year ago filed a motion for the adjudicated facts. We appreciate that the -- this Chamber, Your Honour, has finally ruled on that motion almost a year later. We wish the Chamber had been more expansive in the adjudicated facts found, but that's where we are. If it means that we have to re-litigate and litigate again and again issues and facts that have been determined in other cases, that again makes this case much less efficient. We have tried and spent a considerable amount of time trying to reach agreed facts with the Defence to find out if there were things that are not disputed, that we don't need to take courtroom time to present evidence, that the issues could be narrowed, that there really is not a dispute that a particular village was attacked on a particular day. There really is not a dispute that this woman and her children were evicted from her home in the middle of the night. That's not really disputed. We've done everything we can to narrow the issues. We have tried -- that didn't go anywhere unfortunately, Your Honour. It didn't lead into any significant results. Five filed numerous motions under 92 bis for the admission of written testimony, written evidence. Those have been denied to date. So that is no fault of the Prosecution. We have tried -- we have sought the pre-trial admission of exhibits through the motions we have filed since last fall to admit the ECMM documents, to admit the Spanish Battalion documents, to admit other documents. We have tried to do that because I heard many people say over the last couple years why can't this be done pre-trial? Why do we have to waste trial time on these kind of things? So this Prosecution team tried to take an innovative approach and deal with those issues before trial. Unfortunately, our efforts were denied. Our response and our reply to the Defence trial briefs and whether our filing, Your Honour, on that is accepted or not, our position remains the same. The Defence trial briefs, with all respect, do not comply with Rule 65 ter (F). That Rule specifically requires the Defence to say which specific issues in the case are disputed and why. And I invite the Chamber to look at that Rule again. The language of that Rule. I submit respectfully, Your Honour, it could not have been, it could not have been the intention of the drafters to simply accept a generic "we deny everything." If a we deny everything response is acceptable, if that's an acceptable approach then the Rule 65(F) is meaningless and indeed as Your Honour says these cases cannot be tried efficiently because we're going to waste a huge amount of time, Your Honour, for the Prosecution to prove things that at the end of the day will not real be -- have been disputed. But there's been no -- there's been no requirement for the Defence to comply with Rule 65 ter (F) and accept -- we dispute everything. As Your Honour knows, unfortunately comparisons to Nuremberg are rather meaningless because the proceedings -- the procedures at Nuremberg were entirely different than the proceedings at the ICTY. As Your Honour has said, all parties, including the Prosecution, are entitled to a fair trial. If the Chamber does not allow the Prosecution an adequate opportunity to present its case, then of course the Prosecution will be denied a fair trial. If insufficient evidence is allowed to prove the Prosecution case and the 92 bis motions by the Defence the issue of the sufficiency of the evidence is raised and if the evidence indeed allowed by the Chamber has been too limited and too narrow, the Prosecution might even find itself in the situation of agreeing with the Defence that based on the limitations on its case placed by the Court we have not been able to present a sufficient case. The alternative to many of these things, Your Honours, is to be more creative, and this trial team, this Prosecution team is prepared to do that. We do not have to be wed to the most conservative common law system and I say that, Your Honour, as a common lawyer. I practised in the common law system for the past 25, 26 years. But I can tell you that I am personally not wed to that system, and we need to be more creative in this institution. More evidence in writing is one way to proceed instead of calling all these witnesses live. We might even consider something like a modified dossier, a dossier per crime base with all the witness statements, all the exhibits for that particular crime base, for example, Prozor, in a dossier that would be presented to the Defence and we would ask the Defence again to tell us in that dossier exactly what is disputed, and on the basis of that we can decide which evidence would need to be presented. Now, we can be more creative and we can make -- we can try this case efficiently or we can do it the most conservative, old-fashioned way. My point is Your Honour you will find in this particular time team a willingness to be creative and innovative and try to move this case forward effectively. And we are more willing to work with you in that regard. However, at the end of the day we have to decide how best to present our case and meet our burden of proof, and meet our responsibility to the international community, to meet our responsibility to the victims who deserve for justice to be done. I'll leave that, Your Honour, as I say our provisional response to Your Honour's thoughts this morning and I'm sure we can make a fuller response on the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, too. I listened to you carefully, and everything you have said is very reasonable. Indeed, if the Trial Chamber had granted all the requests pursuant to 92 bis or to judicial notice, it would have made things easier and we would have moved ahead, but there are two parties to a trial, you and the Defence, and if the Defence told us, "We agree, or a judicial notice is requested but this is not okay for us because this impacts on the liability of my client," I as a Judge have to take this into account. You see, that's the problem. That's really where the problem lies. The Rules have provided from ways of really moving fast, but it can only move fast if everybody plays the same game. But if the Defence teams tell us we don't agree, well, the provisions of the Rules cannot really work. But I want to react to what you said because it was very interesting, and I really invite the Defence to think it over. In the Prozor annex, you have 175 facts. They are described in turn. It would indeed be very interesting if the Defence were to take a stance. Look at it. You have fact 133, fact 152. You list people who were killed during the attack. If the Defence were not to challenge the fact that these people were killed, this would mean that we can move ahead. It simply says that during the attack the HVO killed, and that's where the problem is. Either you admit that these people were killed by HVO forces, possibly during fighting or otherwise, I don't know, but if you were to admit that we could really progress. And there is a host of indications if the Defence were to agree or may -- means of moving forward. Another example. Of course this is much more sensitive, because it is alleged that some people were sexually abused or raped. There again, it is challenged or it is admitted. If it were to be admitted, the only problem for everyone is to see who is responsible, to see command responsibility in that. As was stated by Mr. Scott, we must be creative. That is for sure. In the indictment with regard to municipalities, you can see that in some villages dozens of houses were burned down, looted. It would not be necessary in my view to have four or five witnesses who would come and say the same thing. One is enough. But it is up to the Prosecution to say one -- this witness is enough. I don't need the other four. Creativity should also be the province of the Defence, not just the Prosecution. So at this stage I really am curious to hear the Defence teams. Let's starts with Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, good morning. The Prosecution says we should be creative. I say to them they should be more fair. As we speak today they are still out in the field investigating their case. They chose the time when they wanted to issue the indictment, what they wanted to include in the indictment. They designed the indictment in the fashion in which they did. They amended it in a way that includes every single mode of liability including the one that was created by this Tribunal, the joint criminal enterprise, and here they have the nerve to stand up and say that they're being creative and we're -- simply are the ones that are stalling. I've tried being creative in the previous case. I was told we have to stay by the rules. And of course when the Prosecution wanted to be creative, I insisted that they play by the rules as well. I have no problem with thinking outside the box. I think that's the best approach. However, I do believe that we have to put first and foremost the rights of our accused ahead of anything else. In the past this Tribunal has gone on with cases that were level 1 for years on end. I can point to one in particular that is going on at the moment or just finished. It should have been a six-month trial. The problem with that is if you're an outsider, you tend to look and say, well, is this person getting a longer trial, a fairer trial, because of his nationality, whereas in another case there are fewer resources, you being pressed. I don't know. I don't want to speculate. I don't want to go there. The bottom line though is that those case that is preceded us back in the mid-1990s, late 1990s, obviously there was more money for preparation. There was more time, there was more patience. The Security Council now tells us, finish by 2008. That is an impossibility. All you need to do is the numbers. When you look at the cases that are waiting to go to trial and you look at the size, it's an impossibility. It won't happen under any circumstances if there are going to be fair trials. Judge hunt indicated that if the UN does not have the money or the intestinal fortitude to provide fair trials for those that they wish to accuse and try, then they shouldn't set up tribunals. I support Judge Hunt's position. The Security Council established this institution. They should finance. The Prosecution has the right and the discretion to charge individuals and to charge them in the fashion in which they wish. The Security Council curtailed Madam Del Ponte's or the Prosecutor's powers to some extent in that the Bureau now, or at one point, had to intervene to see whether certain cases were within the sort of cases that should be tried before this Tribunal versus cases that should be tried at the state courts. The problem is that the Prosecution in this Tribunal, and you have literature from Judges more or less speaking about this, these tribunals have been used not for the purposes or for the sole purpose of trying an individual to see whether that individual committed crimes but in order to get to the historical truth, for reconciliation purposes, and I think somehow this Tribunal, and I spoke of all of us that are involved in this Tribunal, have lost sight of the fact that this is nothing more than an international criminal court. That's all it is. We're not going to get to any historical truth here. It's impossible. Why? Because at the moment you're cutting deals with the accused to plead out to certain things or some accused or some suspects are not charged and others are, where governments don't cooperate and provide all the documents, where the Prosecution can't get a hold of all the documents on time, and vice versa. It makes it virtually impossible to get to the historical truth. Therefore, I think we need to step back and realise this is nothing more than a criminal court where some international laws are applied and a procedure that evolves. I'd like to say that the rules change as the game is being played. Now, as long as the rules are not changed too much and it doesn't hurt either side it's not a problem, but if we're going to the extent to change the rules where it impacts one party or the other, there I could have a problem. Speaking of changing the rules, I certainly don't object, by the way, if Your Honour wants to take the lead on questioning. The more I -- the more I'm in these cases the more I appreciate the romano-jurudique [phoen], and particularly the French system where you have an investigative Judge. And that's the problem. When they talk about having a dossier, this Prosecution cannot be treated as an investigative judge. They have no obligation to search for exculpatory evidence. They have an obligation to turn it over if they come into possession of it. But they certainly don't commence an investigation in trying to find -- in a balanced fashion. They have a target in mind. They proceed with that target. They collect evidence accordingly. They decide who they're going to investigate, who they're going to talk to, what evidence they're going to collect. And so, to say that somehow they can come up with a dossier at this point in time I'm afraid that I would not be very -- I wouldn't welcome that idea only because I'm suspect of it. They talk about agreed facts and adjudicated facts. When you look at those facts, certainly they're all to the disadvantage of the accused and all to the advantage of the Prosecution. In previous cases, the other lawyers had other tactics. There was maybe fewer documents to worry about. Certainly there are different tactics. And also when you look at the indictments, they didn't have what we have in our particular indictment. So how can I possibly accept an adjudicated fact if the Judge was labouring under less evidence, perhaps less creative lawyering. I don't know. All I know is that I represent a client, and that client is entitled to the full rights just as all the other rights that have preceded my client and the ones that will follow. I don't think that we can try this case within two years. I really don't think that. I would like to do it in two years. But it can be done. Now, how can it be done? I think the only possible way that it can be done is for the Prosecution to go back to the drawing board and to amend that indictment and to cut the sails in. Now, why do I say that? I say that because if you look at the indictment very carefully, paragraph 17 sticks to mind. For me it's that paragraph 17.1 because it discusses Dr. Prlic. Again, they have indicted and charged on every conceivable mode of liability. As Your Honour has aptly pointed out to the Prosecution, surely they must have had some evidence in mind, some documents, some witnesses in mind when they said that he planned, he committed, he aided and abetted, that would go specifically to that particular mode of liability. Or have they done as we call in America thrown everything in including the kitchen sink hoping something might stick. Everything in the alternative. Therefore it's as if I'm shadow boxing throughout the whole trial figuring out, where is that moving target going to be. So they could very well if they want to be creative and if they want to be fair go back and cut it. His Honour asked them to provide a proofing chart, a real proofing chart, one that demonstrates with specificity where each document goes and I think if the Prosecution were to do that, it would then allow us to do what they're asking us to do, which is to say with specificity what we challenge. But I dare say when they submit a pre-trial brief with all those other documents and we're trying to -- we have to sort it out, and they're asking us to more or less lay out our defence in advance of their case so that he can do his rebuttal of my case in his case in chief where I don't think that's a fair process, and to some extent in court we do have an adversarial process. The Prosecution does have the burden of proof. I'm not here to make his life any easier. In fact, I'm here to make it harder. Let's be honest about it. I'm not here to be unfair to him. I'm here to help you, Your Honour, sort out the facts so that at the end of the day you can make a valid, honest, and appropriate decision based on the facts by taking the facts and applying the law in reaching a just decision. So I don't think that the Prosecution is fair when they try to shift the blame on the Defence. I understand that Mr. Scott and his team have been working very, very hard, and I commend them. I can assure you that they're working hard as we speak, and they will continue to work. They will continue to gather evidence. How can I, on earth, then say to you that I can comply within a certain time period if at the same time they're continuing to gather evidence because they're not quite sure what their evidence is? They're still hoping to find some smoking gun, some document, something after all these years. It's not as if I'm working within a particular amount of documents and witnesses that I can rely on and say "this is the case." Getting back also to being creative and this dossier, this is why I appreciate more and more the civil law system. At the pre-trial stage I have absolutely no ability to somehow influence the level investigation. I can't say to the Prosecution, "By the way, you should talk to these witness or collect this evidence." Okay? I'm not there. They've decided to approach their case in the manner in which they did. Fine and dandy. That's their prerogative. Obviously they're not can have depth about their case because they continue to investigate. Did they give us assurances today that they will stop the investigation completely, that they will no longer go out in the field and question witnesses, that they will no longer gather evidence, that this is the bundle of evidence within which we have to work with? I dare say they cannot and they will not do that. Nor do they have to do that because they have a particular obligation, and they are entitled to a fair process as well. And I understand that and I appreciate that. On the other hand you have to appreciate our position. Every time they go out and meet with a new witness I've got to send somebody out there to see whether that witness is telling the truth. Every time they gather evidence I have to check that evidence and see, is there something else that they failed to collect because again as I have to point out, they don't have to collect exculpatory evidence. It's not like the ICC and it's certainly not like the former Yugoslavia where at least there investigative judges and Prosecutors were from a different mindset. I don't want to impugn this Prosecution team, but surely they're not here to help us. They have a result in mind. Their entire case is motivated by that result. Their entire procedure is motivated by that result. They want to get a conviction on each and every charge, and I'm not going to make it any easier. I will make concessions where I think there's no need for me to -- to argue a point if for the sake of arguing. I believe the only thing I need to ask myself each and every time I stand up is the question am I asking or the argument that I'm putting forward, is it relevant to the case? Is it helpful to the trier of fact in order to benefit my case? That's what -- that's what motivates me, that one single question: Is what I'm doing relevant? Nothing more, Your Honour. So I don't have much more to say. I believe Ms. Alaburic was very, very eloquent in talking about the politics of the Security Council. I don't want to go over that all over again, but I do agree with everything she has said, and I don't think this is about politics. This is about several individuals that the Prosecution would like to see die in prison. That's their motive, especially with my particular client. The kind of sentence that they will stand up and argue at the end of the trial is that this man die in prison. And when I look at that, that's what motivates me. That's what gets me up every morning and makes me come over here and think, no, not today. You're not going to have him. I'm not going to make any concessions. You prove your case. If you can prove it, fine; if not, move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before the break we have another five minutes. Do you want to use the five minutes? Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to fit within the five minutes. The question that you have raised today whether it is possible to complete this trial within two years, whether it is possible to complete this task, my answer to that question is this is an impossible mission. This cannot be done without this condition that Mr. Karnavas spoke about, namely the Prosecution needs to reduce the indictment drastically or do something else that would facilitate our work, that is to say get rid of alternative charges, because it is precisely these alternative charges, as Mr. Karnavas said, that mean that we are unable to accept adjudicated facts from other cases because those facts had been determined in a totally different context. Another matter that I wanted to say is that I believe it impossible, unacceptable and irreconcilable with the concept of the fair trial to complete this trial within two years, because the witnesses offered by the Prosecution are enough to take the two-year period. That alone will take the two-year period. However, there is something else that we have to bear in mind. It is not just the fair trial that needs to be ensured, but it is also important to establish facts which would significantly reflect upon the future of the area from which the accused in this case hail. These facts are very important. They will have long-term impact on what will be happening in future in that area. This is precisely the reason why we may not and should not say that this trial must be completed within two years. We have to look for ways to extend that deadline, and this is something that we have to say loud and clear today. Let me reiterate that I believe this to be an impossible task. The Defence of Mr. Bruno Stojic has done everything to ensure that there should not be one day's delay in this trial. I accepted lead counsel. Mr. Murphy was elected yesterday. We did not seek for a day of adjournment, and we found ourselves in the situation where we had 9.700 documents and CDs. In order to open just one single document, you need three minutes. This can give you an idea of what efforts the Defence of Mr. Stojic, as well as all other Defence teams in this case, put in, in order to ensure that this trial proceedings proceed smoothly. I can have some understanding for the position of the Prosecution, because I was a prosecutor for 17 years myself. Therefore, I can understand some of the things they are doing and the reasons for that. I hesitate to use harsh words, but I have to use them. It is irresponsible to accused the Defence of failing to accept certain facts or certain charges in the indictment. Our accused have not been indicted for specific crimes. They cannot be expected to say whether certain Bosniaks were killed in Prozor and by who, because most often our accused do not know that. The burden of proof lies on the Prosecution, and it is the Prosecution who has to prove whether it is so or not. Finally, in conclusion, I wish to say this: Up to today, and let us exclude today's date because we received a new document from the Prosecution, but up to today, we were told by the Prosecution that among the first witnesses we will have two witnesses and one expert witness. We did not receive any statements concerning these two witnesses. As for the expert witness report, we received it only five days ago. We are supposed to start the trial which the Prosecution has been preparing for two or eight years, if not longer, and we are supposed to enter the courtroom in the situation where we have no information on our first witnesses. We are just being given that now, and we can only begin our work now. I think that this is the proper moment to say that this trial cannot be concluded within two years. Nobody can expect us to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now 10.30. We have to have a technical break. We shall resume at ten to eleven, and I'll give the floor to Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to be brief. First of all, I'm kindly asking you to permit me to speak in my own language. It will be easier and probably a bit more precise. Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] First of all, I fully agree with what has already been said by my colleagues Mr. Karnavas and Ms. Nozica, and I join in what they have said, so I will try and avoid any repetition. I also agree with all the theses put forward with regard to the completion strategy that you yourself mentioned, Your Honour, and your starting point in the deliberations, in fact, and especially bearing in mind your assertions about the potential possibilities open to the Tribunal in curtailing the time that many the trial will take. However, as you yourself stated, and I think that you quoted His Honour Judge May, over and above all those requirements for an expeditious, speedy and rational trial and especially in view of the closing strategy is the requirement for a fair trial. And on the list of all the principles that the trial must subscribe to is that it must be a fair and just trial. I don't think I need elaborate this principle, because if we continue the proceedings and comply with the founders, the Security Council deadlines, and the trial is not fair, then the trial will have served no purpose. So there's no dilemma on that score whatsoever. Now, looking at the substance of the matter, the length of a trial in all trials throughout the world, and this Tribunal is no exception and can be no exception to legal proceedings throughout the world, the duration of each trial is determined by the indictment. The Prosecution has all the legal prerogatives to define and give shape to the indictment, and it functions not only on the basis of the principle of legality but also has the right to function and is indeed doing so at this Tribunal as well on the principle of opportune-ness. So that is to say that you hold somebody responsible for something that you have proof and evidence about and which satisfies other parameters, a minimum above the perimeters, the interests of justice, the interests of the victims, and so on and so forth. In the Kupreskic trial, for example, where we were dealing with the Croatian-Muslim conflict in Bosnia in 1993, it was not an international conflict, it did not plead that. But in Kordic and Cerkez and Blaskic as well, those trials, is not to be found in any of these trials. In Halilovic, in Hadzihasanovic, for example, in those cases it -- the indictment was very rational, very narrow, and just a few relative facts were selected and the indictment was constructed on those few facts. And I can say that otherwise it would be too broad. So the indictment defines and determination the duration of a trial. All other measures and considerations which could be used in one extent or another without infringing upon the principal notion of a fair trial can have their influence. Depending on our conventions, they can have a 5 per cent influence a 10 or 15 per cent influence, but they cannot have a greater influence than 15 to 20 per cent, let's say. The Prosecution, in what it said a moment ago, stated that this Trial Chamber, this Tribunal, the Court or the Pre-Trial Judge did not allow the Prosecution to use all its creative potential and instruments which could abridge the duration of the trial. We're talking about adjudicated facts, for example, notorious facts, introducing 100 witnesses into the record of these proceedings, and so on and so forth. I don't want to enter into that realm. My colleague, Mr. Karnavas, has presented arguments as to the limitations of things like that. There was no joint criminal enterprise, he said, and so on and so forth. He raised those issues. The Prosecution is in fact striving for a -- written proceedings, if I can put it that way, to my mind. Now, attorneys, whether we come from the common law system or civil law system, we all know that written submissions and written proceedings or, rather, proceedings which to a large extent evolve through documents and written material, the keeping of records and so on and so forth is more or less applied in civilian matters, civilian lawsuits but not in criminal trials and I think the general optimism displayed by the Prosecution at this Tribunal is based around the use of material from previously adjudicated facts in previous trials, through one form or another, and that they are very optimistic in their hopes, because when we come to a specific case and see the differences that exist and why some material can be used whereas other material cannot be used in one particular case, then we see that we come across a series of problems and limitations. We either have to forget the principle of a fair trial in order to neutralise those limitations and be able to use more material from other trials or do something else. So what I'm saying is the possibilities of shortening the trial the duration of the trial are very modest. You can apply them, but just to a very small measure, make them have a very small influence on the case. Everything else, 90 per cent of the legal proceedings that follow are the result of an indictment. And what we speak of an indictment in this specific case, I would like to say the following: The Prosecution on the one side says we have to use and endeavour to use material from other trials, records, statements of witnesses, adjudicated facts, things like that, undisputed facts, unchallenged facts, and things like that; whereas on the other hand it is not willing and does not wish or, rather, is ignoring the possibility of taking a realistic stock of the state of affairs in those trials, and in this trial in particular. For example, in this particular trial, all six accused or, rather, the time-span of the indictment and the events taking place in the indictment from 1991, from the Dayton Accords -- up to the Dayton Accords in 1994. The Washington Agreement in 1994, I meant, yes. This -- and it is stated that the conflict between the Bosnian and Herzegovinian Muslims and the Bosnia-Herzegovinian Croats, in fact, starts -- that is the construction of the joint criminal enterprise effectively control and so on, starts with 1991. Now, in the trials that I mentioned a moment ago, it was established, although the limits were not clearly defined, when you enter into the details of the judgements it was established in Blaskic, in Kordic, in Kupreskic, in all those trials, in Naletelic, perhaps I have omitted to mention some trial, it was established that this conflict, this conflict, which is backbone of this indictment, the Muslim-Croat conflict in Bosnia, is in fact the year 1993. So of those three calendar years contained in the indictment, the Prosecution, of course, is going to refer back to the other cases, those that suit him, that we should actually deal with 1993 alone. That's the only pertinent year. Now, Your Honour, from the standpoint of the Defence, if the Prosecution in this trial and before this Trial Chamber presents the fact that our accused were in fact in some criminal domain already in 1991, at least in the sense of mens rea and in the sense of creating plans in 1991 and through 1992 for them -- for a conflict to have taken place in 1993, I have to defend that case. First of all, I have to defend the fact that without joint criminal -- joint criminal enterprise, I have to return to mens rea. I have to return to 1991 because the Prosecutor is beginning his story from 1991 and especially because of joint criminal enterprise and responsibility, I have to go back to 1991, deal with the whole of 1992 to look at the conflict in 1993 when the material events are charged and deal with actus reus. So I have to deal with that whole issue. What I want to say by quoting that example is that if the Prosecutor has provided us with that kind of framework, then the Defence has to respond to that kind of framework otherwise it will be incompetent or it won't be doing its job properly, and the result of that will be a trial that isn't fair and isn't just. So in one way or another, it is the position of the Prosecution that this is not their problem and that this trial must last as long as the minimum time that you have calculated for it, and I have to say, Your Honour, with all due respect that I seem to feel that in your assessments and arithmetic you were very optimistic, quite obviously there is something amiss here, because the duration of this trial, regardless of all the measures that can be taken, can be availed of, deter -- is determined by the length of the indictment and the contents of the indictment and that is not the fault -- if I can use the word fault, it's not the fault of the Trial Chamber. That is to say that the accused and that the Defence cases will step outside the time span of the Security Council, but the problem is that the indictment was raised in such a manner from the very beginning that quite obviously that calendar and the amount of time given to it will not be sufficient for the trials to be completed. It is up to the Trial Chamber and the Court to determine what is more important, what is higher up on the list of priorities, whether closing strategy imposed by the founders of the Tribunal or a fair and just trial imposed by the needs to hold a trial and to hold legal proceedings in the first place. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give you the floor, but for a few minutes only.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, as I have always presented my position, I just need six sentences Your Honour and the first of them is this: These legal proceedings started in April 2004 when the indictment was raised. In view of everything that has been said in the courtroom so far it would emerge that the trial will not be completed by the end of 2008 in conformity with the UN Security Council Resolution. So I don't think that any further deliberations as to who would be to blame for this for us finishing the trial on -- on time or not are not bearing fruit. I think that it is -- a fundamental problem for these proceedings in this courtroom is the concept of the Defence cases and the concept of the defence and that is through a rationalisation of time, and I'm not going to stipulate all the forms of responsibility and accountability of our accused in this trial, but it is important because every fact, absolutely every fact from the so-called crime base refers to the events and acts committed by our accused, and that kind of indictment determines the Defence case. Therefore, you cannot accept the Defence teams to be cooperative in the way in which the Prosecution would expect them to be, because any cooperativeness in this -- along those lines would go to the detriment of our clients. Furthermore, the Court cannot satisfy the demands of the Prosecution that most of the crime base facts be solved by the -- by written motions and written evidence, because that would mean acts on the part of the accused and the Rules do not allow for this type of presentation of evidence. Now, a solution is to amend the indictment. I don't want to bring that question up again, but let me just give you an example. On the 16th of November, we had an amended indictment. In another trial before this same Tribunal, one of the forms of accountability and what our accused are charged with. I'm going to say this in English because it's easier for me to do so, aiding and abetting in a joint criminal enterprise. And 16 days prior to that on the 1st of November, 2005, in the Cermak Markac case, the indictment -- the Prosecution deleted from the indictment charges and provisions related to the aiding and abetting and joint criminal enterprise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully comply with what my colleagues have said. I don't want to waste any more of your time but just one sentence from me. Is seems that it is quite obvious that there are just two ways in which the duration of this trial can be shortened. One is to reduce the indictment and the second is possibly to sever the trials. The accused Valentin Coric, the Defence did put in a motion to that effect, to have severance, whereas it was rejected by the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't want to repeat what my colleagues before me have already stated. I think Mr. Karnavas put it all before you very nicely. Of course it is in the interests of the Defence teams to have speedy and efficacious trial. However, that can be at the detriment of a fair and just trial, and at the detriment of our clients. I'm just afraid of one thing that might crop up during this trial if we were to limit the duration, and this is true for the Prosecution as well, that the Defence and the Prosecution would work under a certain amount of pressure, and I'd like to compare it to a game of chess. If you have time pressure, you can make moves that are very often not reasonable and can be detrimental to your defence. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give the floor back to Mr. Scott. I should like to thank all the Defence counsel for having assessed the situation and provided their personal viewpoint. Mr. Scott were certainly respond to some of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll be very short. The Defence took a total of 39 minutes to make their various responses and so far I've used 7 minutes, but I will just use, if I can, about three more minutes. Your Honour, if you listened well over the last few minutes, you ever heard each Defence team say that they are not interested in working efficiently. They are not interested in working creatively. They are not interested in doing anything to make this case work more properly or more efficiently. In fact Mr. Karnavas said it quite explicitly. His goal is to make it as difficult as possible for the Prosecution to present its case. We raise the issue of Rule 65 ter (F) before and I do want to spend 30 seconds more on it. What the Rule requires is that when the Defence filed their pre-trial brief in response to the Prosecution brief that they set out the following: 1, in general terms the nature of the accused's defence; number 2, the matters with which the accused takes issue in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief; and, 3, in the case of each such matter, the reason why the accused takes issue with it. Now, of course the Defence don't want to do that, and let's -- as Mr. Karnavas says let's be very transparent. We're all adults in this courtroom. What the Defence hope, Your Honour, is by stretching out this case, by making it as -- as Mr. Karnavas says, as making it as difficult as possible for the Prosecution case, at some point you will bring the hammer down and you will make -- you will cut the Prosecution case. Now, what more could any Defence team want? They know if they stretch this case out, if they make it as difficult as possible for us to present our case it will be to the detriment of the Prosecution. That's very easy for anyone to see. So the response is, of course, let's not enforce Rule 65 ter (F) let's certainly not do that. Let's not do anything to try and narrow and identify the bona fide disputed issues. Let's not do that. Let's not do anything to work efficiently. Let's try to make the system work as slowly and as difficult as possible and at the end of the day we'll get the Judge to make the Prosecution cut its case, to make the Prosecution cut its evidence. What more could any Defence team want? Ladies and gentlemen, if we just stick to our guns and make -- drag these proceedings out and make it as difficult as possible, the Prosecution will have to give up its case. The Prosecution will have to cut the indictment. The Prosecution will have to call less evidence. What more could any Defence team want? And that is not a fair trial for the Prosecution, for the international community, or for the victims. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just have one moment just to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [In English] Few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Few minutes, few minutes. This sort of reminds me of that film, Cool Hand Luke, with Paul Newman, where at the end there is that famous saying, what we have here is a failure of communication. I was speaking English. Mr. Scott is a native English speaker. I don't know how he interpreted or misinterpreted what I had to say. When I said that I had -- it's my job to make it difficult for him to get a conviction, it he thinks that I'm here as the grease on the prosecutorial wheels, so he can come in here, sashay, throw a few pieces of evidence around, and he's going to walk away with my client being in prison for the rest of his life, he's sadly mistaken. This Prosecution and the way that the Prosecution office is set up at the ICTY is classic common law. They're not here for the truth as far as I'm concerned. They're here to get a conviction. The result --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour, this is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He is here -- he is here to get a conviction. If he were for the truth, then why am I getting today this evidence right now with respect to one witness, Mr. Donia, that I'm going to have to sift through? Today I finally get the list of five witnesses. They knew well in advance. I could have had that months ago. And they're going to sit here and tell you that they're here to play fair. They're here to be creative, where if this is being creative, well, I have news for them. This is a way of trying to obstruct the Defence.
