This is a way to prevent me from doing my job, and my job is to make sure that if he gets that conviction he's going to have to work for it. He's going to have to prove that case here. He cannot have an indictment where he just throws everything in, every mode of liability, and say, pick and choose, Your Honour. You figure it out. And for the first time, this Prosecution is faced with a -- with a Pre-Trial Judge who is saying no. You drafted that indictment. You put all those modes of liability. You came up with those 9.000 documents, and by God you tell us where each and every one of those documents fits within the indictment and don't expect the Trial Chamber or the Defence to try to figure it out. And I'm offended by the way the Prosecution seems to think that it's the fault of the Defence. And if it's not the Defence, he blames the Trial Chamber. If the Trial Chamber had only accepted all those adjudicated facts or if all those 92 bis statements had come in. They can reduce the indictment. They can make it fairer for everyone. Nothing prevents them from pinpointing exactly what it is they think they can prove. And if they knew what they were going to be able to prove they wouldn't be out there investigating. And I remind the Court that this Prosecution is not the same as a Prosecution would be in a civil law system. They're not magistrates. They're parties. They're advocates, just like the Defence, and there lies the difference, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's all calm down. Just a point of detail. You mentioned Rule 65 ter (F). As you know, once the Prosecutor has filed its exhibit in paragraph (E), the charge orders the Prosecution to file a preliminary brief that specifies the -- and the reasons for which they are wanting to challenge it. In general terms the nature of the accused's defence, matters with which the accused takes issue, and the case of each method or reason why the accused takes issue with it. I have looked into the pre-trial brief very carefully, those presented by both parties. I realised that each accused was challenging any form of responsibility and stipulated that from thereon they challenged everything. So it is impossible under those conditions to reach a consensus on any of the facts or any questions of law, because the whole -- everything is challenged. This is not the first time that this occurs in a trial. In a previous trial where Mr. Mundis was on the Prosecution team, Mr. -- the case against Mr. Hadzihasanovic, the Defence team had challenged everything also. So when the Defence challenges everything, then of course it is important for the Prosecution to prove by calling its witnesses and presenting its exhibits everything that is charged in the indictment. Everybody has understood that after this roundtable everybody has spoken openly and freely. I enabled each counsel to clearly state his or her position, and it seems clear that the ball is now in the court of the Prosecution. It's for the Prosecution to understand what it is it is wanting to do, how does it intend to proceed over the next few months, over the next few years to present its case. The Defence will also be allowed enough time to present its case. This is why I feel it is important for Madam Carla Del Ponte in person to come and tell us how she thinks this case should be presented. In the history of this Tribunal, this will be a trial involving a great number of accused. In the Kupreskic case, there were very few facts, whereas in this case, this is quite a different story. We are now starting on these trials which involve a great number of accused, and the Prosecution should tell us how much time they need. It is my responsibility to remind you that a Resolution has been passed by the Security Council. A number of issues may arise. And as Madam Prosecutor goes to the Security Council to explain what she is doing, she could come here and tell us how she thinks this case should unfold. It's all very well to travel around Europe and catch fugitives. It is important to have an overall view of the way in which the cases are being presented, particularly in a case where everybody has reminded us here we have approximately 10.000 exhibits and, for the time being, 400 witnesses. So maybe we -- things will be clearer after the 12th of April. I would now like to address the other items on the agenda. One item which I indicated to you has to do with the state of health of the accused. I feel that I -- as a Judge, I have a personal responsibility here throughout the trial to bear in mind the state of health of the accused. That is the way I understand things. If an accused is affected by some illness or another, I would like the Defence counsels to let me know about this on a confidential basis, ex parte, confidential, whichever way they prefer, and let me know that one or another accused has one or another affliction. If I receive no document or no filing, I will conclude that everybody is in a good state of health. This is what I hope for. But if a problem were to arise I would like you to let me know as soon as possible. I wanted to make sure that this was recorded, to make sure that everybody is informed as they should be. When a trial is that long, it is important to address this particular issue. The other item I would like to raise, which is an important one, I had asked the Defence and the Prosecution, the lawyers, to meet and to address the issue of the length of the cross-examination once the Prosecution will have questioned the -- all of it's witnesses. I don't think that much progress has been made. Nonetheless, I shall give you the floor to both parties, because as I mentioned last time, if the Prosecution questions a witness -- let's me take the case -- or let me refer to the witness list and take the case of Witness 2 viva voce, a live witness, number 2 on the witness list. As far as this witness, Witness 2 is concerned, the Prosecution had planned to question it for an hour and a half, because this witness will testify on points 1, 8, 9, 10, 18, 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 16, 17, and 22, referring to paragraphs 101 and 108. The Prosecution had planned one and a half hours for this. It's assumed that the witness would come tomorrow. What does the Defence do in term of its cross-examination? Does that mean that each Defence counsel will take an hour and a half to cross-examine the witness, or will one Defence counsel act as the lead counsel on behalf of the other counsels, or one or other counsel could intervene if there were ancillary or alternative questions. I think everybody's understood this clearly. When I base my calculation on three months and -- three years and four days, my calculations was based on an equal time for both parties. If it's an hour and a half for this particular witness for the Prosecution, then the Defence also gets an hour and a half. But if each party wants to use this hour and a half, it's not three years that the trial is going to last but 18 years. So everybody understands what's at stake here I'm sure. In 18 years' time, there is a fair chance that I will no longer be around. So I would like to know whether between the counsels have had an opportunity to exchange their views on this and whether any progress has been made because the lengths of the trial depends on this issue also. Mr. Scott or Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Regrettably the parties have made no further progress since the last Status Conference on this issue although clearly there have been a number of different pleadings by the parties on the best way to proceed, and I believe that's the most up-to-date information concerning the positions of the various parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Aside from the pleadings where I think we're more or less in agreement on the Defence, I can report that four team met last night. That was the latest. Unfortunately, two of our -- the two teams -- the other teams were not available. But this issue did come up and we had a fairly lengthy discussion regarding this, all with the understanding that we need to -- we the Defence need to discipline ourselves to make sure that -- that we live within a certain time limit, at the same time represent our respective clients. The end result is as follows and I now repeat what I said earlier, because I echoed in last night, that we should only be asking questions that are relevant to our particular case. Now, if you look at the indictment, you would see that about 90 -- 85 per cent of the case, because of the joint criminal enterprise, affects everyone, and then you have that 15 per cent with respect to the individuals. Some of the witnesses only need to be questioned by one or two of the -- of the accused, because it only affects them. So I think from the Defence stand point, we believe that the best way to approach it is as follows: One, among ourselves we would try prior to coming to court to resolve who would take the lead to what extent, what issues need to be addressed, and to proceed accordingly. I can -- I can assure the Trial Chamber, at least with respect to all the major witnesses, because Dr. Prlic is at the apex of this indictment, in all likelihood I'm going to be required to cross-examine most if not all of the witnesses. But again, I go back to what I stated earlier. Every question should be prefaced with one question in mind: How does this further the case? How is this relevant to the case? If it's not relevant, then it's not necessary. And Obviously we agree among ourselves that we should not be repetitive. If an issue has been covered that might affect another accused, there is no sense the other accused standing up and cross-examining. However, there may be an instance where an issue was covered but maybe there is a nuance that needs to be followed up because of the particular defence of another accused. In that instance, it's not repetitive for the other attorney to get up, maybe ask a few prefatory questions, and then zero in on that particular nuance. I think that's the best way to proceed. I do not think that you can possibly come up with some mathematical formula. The Prosecution can get up and put Donia on for one or two hours. I can tell you I need two or three days with the man I'm speaking on a conservative basis. I would say probably twice or three times that amount of time if he's going to stick by what he says. Sometimes you need to beat about the bush a little bit to get the witness to where they're compliant and answer the questions. I'm not saying that's going to be the case with this witness or another witness but it's been my experience that you just can't zero in. Maybe if it's the Trial Chamber asking the question, because you sit much higher than the rest of us and there seems to be a different relationship between the Trial Chamber and the witness, they might be more forthcoming. But sometimes when comes to the lawyers, depending on how the witness may have been coached or the agenda that the witness may have, they're going to be less responsive and that means I have to work a little bit harder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe you spoke on behalf of all the Defence lawyers. And as you stated on this point, one thing is obvious. The Defence counsel must meet, and as you said, they must appoint among themselves one or two who are going to cross-examine a witness. Let me make you a few suggestions. As I said, there are three main points in the indictment, the facts alleges to have been committed in the municipalities, the concept of JCE, and individual liability for each of the accused. As regards the facts, let me go back to Witness 2. He's going to say that in his village of Ristani on the 25th of May, 1993, whilst they were in their flat the HVO came and took them away, and the witness is going to tell what happened. Is it really necessary for the cross-examination to go back, for the witness to say exactly what happened. It would be enough for one lawyer to put a question, in principle at least. So I think that when it comes to this type of facts, it is enough for one lead counsel to settle the issue. Of course if somebody has got a wonderful idea whilst a colleague is cross-examining, the lawyer is free to put a question, but you are all excellent professionals, so I believe that the one who is going to cross-examine will be very thorough. So this could be one solution. Two other points that are also very important in my view. JCE - yeah, I'll give you the floor in a second - and individual criminal liability. This is only logical. When the Prosecution is going to address the overall issue of joint criminal enterprise through their witnesses, I know that each of you will have their own views on this, and it is only logical that each of you can intervene on this. But thereafter, I don't know how the Prosecution is going to go about it but I were the Prosecution, I know what I would have done. If the Prosecution decide to go to the individual liability of each of the accused, as they did in their submissions, of course it's only logical if they take ten hours for Mr. Prlic, Mr. Prlic's lawyer will have at least ten hours too. The other lawyers will be able to speak if they have to intervene, too, as a result. But this is something to be sorted out among yourselves, Defence teams. As a rule in civil law jurisdictions, lawyers agree among themselves to know who is going to speak first, and I believe this is the same thing in common law systems. So you should also be "creative" to avoid problems, because if you play by the book, we'll be here in 18 years' time. All of us. Well, maybe not all of us; some of us, still. Yes, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wish to clarify just one issue which perhaps can lead to problems in the future, which has to do with the situation where one counsel would on behalf of the others cross-examine. This is not what we agreed on. Each of the accused may have his own concept of defence. Therefore, each Defence team will prepare for cross-examination individually, and we will try to cooperate among ourselves in order to rationalise the use of time. So we agreed on the following: If Mr. Karnavas puts a question that we believe to be relevant and we are satisfied with the answer, we will not put additional questions. This is how the Defence teams will be cooperating and rationalising the time. In addition to that, I believe that we need to take into account the relevance of evidence. This is something that we discussed yesterday among Defence teams. In that sense, we can have certain problems, especially when it comes to expert witnesses, because they need to be examined on their expert reports and their testimony in previous cases. We have such examples as expert witnesses in, for example, Milosevic case were examined in direct for 40 minutes and four and a half hours in cross-examination. Therefore, I think we need to be flexible in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may add just two sentences. What my distinguished colleagues Mr. Karnavas and Ms. Alaburic said, it is exactly what we altogether had in mind and I think in that respect we are -- our position is fully justified. The main issue is relevance, and I really don't think that we have to establish some rules which will be controlled by the time. It is relevance. So it well may be there is a witness testifying, for example, two hours, with no questions at all. However, in -- we must foresee the possibility that there will be a possible conflict of Defence's theory. So something which will be relevant for Defence A in crossing the witness will be fine with others but not for somebody else from this Defence, and he perhaps will, or she will have to go towards some other segments of the testimony. So that must be envisaged I believe. And another example that you just mentioned, Witness 2 than kind of testimony, and it is quite a typical one and we should expect quite a lot of such testimonies, my question was the whole example which you put, the witness was there, the HVO entered, he was arrested, he was transported, fine. My only question at that time would be, by who? Who addressed you sir? What was the badge on the uniform? That is all what matters. You of course are aware that my client is a soldier, so under 7, 1 he was there, no. That -- was he assisting anybody? We should see later. Under seven -- Article 7(3) we have to find whether those are his troops. Under joint criminal enterprise theory, I don't need that witness, of course. So it's -- sometimes it's different. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wish to add one matter in relation to what my colleague said. I would like to kindly ask you to bear in mind that in the course of the proceedings we will definitely use only as much time as the Prosecution uses in direct, at least in relation to majority of the witnesses. Some witnesses, of course, will require more time, and there will certainly be witnesses for whom we will have no questions whatsoever. So we need to assess what is relevant for us, and if we do that, I think that ultimately we will realise that we will not be using more time than the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are various types of witnesses. There are expert witnesses. There are victims who will come to testify. There are eyewitnesses who were there because it so happened that they were on that location. There are international witnesses, quite a number of them at that. So for each category of witnesses, the Defence teams may have to put different questions depending on the type of testimony. And you are absolutely right to stress this point, and you precisely have the issue of expert witnesses. Those who will come to testify may have to be cross-examined by all Defence teams in a thorough manner, admittedly, but the Defence teams should make a clear distinction between the types of witnesses. That is the criterion that you will have to adjust to. If I mentioned Witness 2, it is because there are many witnesses falling under this category. This witness might stress the fact that he was arrested, transported, detained, possibly abused. It is up for the Prosecution in putting their questions, but if they are focused questions, so it is up for the Prosecution to give the overall picture, and after that the lead Defence counsel will be able to cross-examine the witness. If he doesn't put all the necessary questions, other teams may put them. But trust the Judges to put questions, because as Judges, we will not leave anything in the dark. Even if you don't put the right questions, the Judge is not partial, is not biased, and his only rationale is the need to establish the truth, and he will put all the right questions. So whatever it may be, when a witness comes to testify, comes to the stand, it must be useful. It is not just to please each party that they are called to the stand. It is for the truth to be established. And the ultimate purpose of testimony, of evidence, is that Judges, based on their relevance and their probative value, may draw some conclusions from such testimony. A Prosecution witness or a Defence witness will be called because there is a purpose in calling such a witness. If the purpose is defeated, why should that witness be called? And if you have an objective, you must focus on it by putting the right questions. Earlier on, quite rightly so, Mr. Kovacic mentioned 7(1) and 7(3). If Witness 2 was arrested by a soldier, we must know who he was arrested by. The issue of the badge is to be raised, and that is a question to be taken care of by the Prosecution. The Prosecution will have to meet those concerns, failing which the Defence will be free to cross-examine. But be aware that the Judges will not leave any doubt about it. We will step in, in order to obtain this type of information. I do invite you to read the decision issued by the Appeals Chamber a few days ago in the Stakic case, and it is clearly stated that at some point in time there was a problem because there was a grey area around one issue, a question, and the Appeals Chamber said that the Defence and the Judges had to put questions. So please trust the Judges that they will know when to put questions to witnesses. I urge you could keep working on this fundamental issue, and you should very shortly find some way of working. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will take that advice to heart and again try to work with the Defence. But if I could, this issue we specifically asked to be again put on the agenda for the Status Conference today for a more particular reason. There are really two issues involved with how this type of cross-examination proceeds. One of them goes to the 18-year possibility, as Your Honour has aptly identified it. That is, it goes to the overall length of the potential proceedings. The other aspects of this problem is a more practical one, and that goes to informing -- for the Prosecution to inform VWS in terms of how to get the witnesses here so that we're not in a situation where we either run out of witnesses are we have witnesses who are waiting for a large number of days and then perhaps have to be sent home and then brought back to The Hague in order to testify. While we certainly can all as professionals appreciate the fact that it is extremely difficult in advance to anticipate how long it might be, and I go back to page 55, lines 2 and 3 where, Mr. Karnavas said, "I do not that I that you can possibly come up with some mathematical formula," the Prosecution does believe, Your Honour, that we must have some kind of rough mathematical formula as a default in order for us to plan to bring the witnesses here. And a couple of examples can easily, I believe, illustrate the situation. We have previously indicated that we will be commencing our case with a number of senior-type witnesses, international witnesses, witnesses that are not the crime base witnesses, Rule 65 ter estimates tend to be on the longer side rather than the one and a half hour witness we discussed a few moments ago. These tend to be witnesses who will be in the box on the Prosecution's side for four hours, five hours, circumstances hours, eight hours even, and so the problem there becomes, Mr. President, when we put the witness on the box knowing that we will take more than one day for the direct examination, will the Defence be entitled one or one and a half days? Will they be entitled three days in total for all of them? Will they be entitled to six days, seven days? Because if we start on a Monday with a one-day witness, do I need to have the witness here for Wednesday, for Thursday, for next week, for two weeks from now? These are the practical implications of at least having some kind of a default; i.e., the Defence in total gets two to one or three to one or one to one or five to one so that I can then tell VWS, "I need the next witness here three days from now or next Monday or two and a half weeks from now." Otherwise we'll be in the situation where we stand up and say we're out of witnesses for the week, unfortunately, or alternatively we will face I mention pressure from the registry after a witness has been waiting here for five or six days to send the witness home because it now appears that it they won't be testifying for four or five additional days. So those are the more practical aspects leaving aside the 18-year problem, the more practical action of why we need some kind of guidance from Your Honour so that we can move the trial as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you set it out perfectly. You really articulated the problem as it is because you have time for the examination-in-chief but you also have to take care of the time when witnesses come. It has to be planned and it's far from being easy. You have perfectly identified the issue and you said that if you have your international witness, if you examine him for eight hours or four hours, I need to know how much time will be granted to the Defence for their cross-examination to know which will be the next witness. You were very clear in defining the problem. For the time being, I am not able to tell you here and now what the final position will be, and I'll tell you why. Because by the 14th of April, I should have your comprehensive document showing the link between the documents, the witnesses, and the facts. By way of an example, I go back to Witness 2. You have scheduled an hour and a half. In your submissions, you were very clear. You have taken up what I'd asked for in my order, the name of the witness, the summary of his testimony, the counts in the indictment, and the paragraphs. The time you would need would be an hour and a half. But when the witness comes to the stand, I still don't know which are the documents you're going to introduce through him. This has to do with alleged events in the village of Ristani. Two people were killed as well. Are you going to introduce documents or not? So I could show you this witness after witness. You were requested to do some work which would help us progress. You might not have any documents for certain witnesses, but regarding others you might have a lot of them, obviously. So will the Defence teams need time to cross-examine witnesses on documents? I mean, as I said, you are excellent professionals on both sides of the wells, and you know in both types of cases the documents may be the most important part. Witnesses -- witness testimony, that's one thing, but it's always a relevant thing. Whereas a document is quite -- has got an important weight. And if a Defence lawyer does their work, well, they're going to focus on documents as well, especially when we have to do with military operations, with orders and the knowledge thereof. So there's going to be some discussion around documents, and this, too, may require a lot of time. I do hope that in the same way as I did, the Defence lawyers have long been busy with the 10.000 documents they have received, and I do hope that they did what I did, that they watched the video footage, because if you failed to do so, you're going to be prejudiced. Now, to answer your question, I'll tell you what I need and what I asked you to provide me with. I wanted to have an idea of the witnesses you intended to call for the next two months. From what I understood, your first witness will be Donia, expert witness Donia. That so? He's going to be your first witness; is that right? Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Thank you. If I could just have a moment, please. If we could go into private session, Your Honours, because some of these witnesses may seek protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in open [as interpreted] session, the Prosecution has told us that a list of witnesses has been handed over to the Defence. This will be communicated to the Chamber as of the 14th of April onwards, as stipulated in the order the calling of these witnesses has -- the calling of this witness has been done in a logical order in order to enable the Bench to have a fair understanding of the case. So this I have noted. But this, nonetheless, does not settle the question of the lengths of all of this. Now, as far as the length is concerned, I am handicapped by the fact that I do not have the other two Judges by my side to discuss it. We -- these two Judges will only step in two weeks before the commencement of trial. So as you can understand, I face this difficulty. I have a point of view, but they might have another point of view. So I cannot vouch for their point of view whatever the case may be. For the time being, you have given us an estimated time for the witness testimony of these witnesses in your submissions. So the only unanswered question is -- relates to the first witness. How much time will the Defence need to cross-examine this first witness? Generally speaking, in all the trials so far in this kind of case, the Defence has as much time as the Prosecution. The only difference lies in the fact that the Prosecution -- the only difference is there are six Defence counsel in compared to the Prosecution. In the case of the first witness, the witness is a victim. Maybe the Defence counsels will agree to -- and see which of the Defence counsel shall cross-examine the witness. I think we should evolve with a degree of flexibility and then we can make the necessary corrections as we go along. As far as the first witness is concerned, the answer I would provide would be this - I haven't had time to look into this, but what -- how much time had you allotted for the first witness? Was it an hour and a half, two hours, or three hours? Two hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I didn't have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two and a half hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On the 65 ter list it should indicate that and that's the number we would be guided by at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So well. So if you have planned to hear this witness for two and a half hours, the Defence should also be entitled to two and a half hours. So if you could sort that out between you and tell us who the lead counsel will be, which lead counsel will be cross-examining this witness, and then we'll proceed on a case-by-case basis, because I cannot settle this issue right now given the fact that this question hinges on the length of the trial. Is this going to take two years, three years, 18 years? I don't know. It's Mrs. Carla Del Ponte's responsibility to tell us what the case might be, yeah. It's for her to answer that question. So we will have an opportunity to get back to this, but I think Mr. Karnavas is eager to take the floor. You have the floor, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a couple of points, Your Honour. First with respect to the first witness, I note that there are two different first names for this particular witness with two different dates of birth. I assume that the Prosecution will tell us whether they're the same person or whether they're two different persons. I don't want to mention their name, but I can bring that up to their attention. With respect to the fourth witness they indicated, I wish to note that -- I guess that's 116 on the 65 ter list. It was only -- this was last week that we received that and we only have one video clip with respect to this particular witness. We don't have any other disclosure material with respect to this witness. I mention this only because if we're to make some kind of prediction of how long it will take for us to cross-examine a particular witness, we need to know in advance, and this is something that we should have had, I dare say, months ago, all of the disclosure material with the particular witness. One last point, because the Prosecution noted, you know, how magnanimous they were that 14 days in advance they provided us with five different names, and that just last week or beginning of this week they gave us two other names that are on the list. They then go on to say that they have a set and logical plan. They've been working on it for a long time. I recall back in November or December when we had one of our Status Conferences, Mr. President, you indicated that you wanted the Prosecution to present their case in a logical fashion where you're dealing with subject matters. When you look at what we're being presented, it's more like a Hollywood production, to start with. If we were in front of a jury, I can understand the very drama of having a video clip and having a victim, and I don't want to minimise. There were victims on all sides in this war, and I would say that all sides behaved poorly on many different occasions. But that's what we have here. And then we have sort of what I would call a ratatouille approach of presenting the case. You have four different witnesses that are going to be all over the place, not necessarily in any particular way of presenting a coherent block or group of a subject matter, as was requested. Again, I just note this because if the Prosecution is going to stand up and continually attack the Defence and try to show how magnanimous they are, let's be honest. They were told to present their case in a particular fashion. They're not doing that. It's their case. They can present it however they wish. But on the other hand, the more complex the way they put it, the more time it's going to need for us to figure out where they're going and how to approach it. That's number one. And number two, I do think that if they have been making this set and logical plan for months in advance, they should have already the blocks, the subject matters in an order in which they want to present it more or less so they can give us sort of an outline of the subject matters and the witnesses so at least we would know that for this group of people, for this subject matter we don't have to worry until maybe next year. That is only fair, because after all as Mr. Scott proudly pronounced that he knows the case -- or the Prosecution knows their case more than anyone else, and they should. It's their case. So why not be a lit bit more trance parent. If they're really after the truth and they really want to be fair to the accused, that's the way to go about it. And also it's fair to the Trial Chamber because you have to participate in the questioning process, as your two other colleagues, and it gives you an opportunity to know where to focus on -- early on so we can all be more efficient. That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just two or three words. In preparing for those witnesses which now we are being informed de jure that it might be this one that is the first one or second. Anyway we know where the priorities are, we are of course parallelly or at the same time doing on disclosures kindly provided to us by the Prosecution office. Well, there is a Rule 68 which is quite oftenly, regrettably mentioned in the courtrooms as well, and my submission is that the Rule 68 material in a bigger part should have been disclosed before many, many months. Sadly, it is not yet. On 16 March, which is what, three weeks from today, or two weeks, we received a letter from the Prosecution informing us that there are new disclosures put on this EDS system, electronic network, and we checked that and there are really two -- two new folders, and just for the record, Your Honour, one of those two folders is Rule 68, so it is obviously very, very late disclosed to us, which contains as the Prosecution said 96 documents. And it is not quite disturbing to hear 96 documents. We're dealing with thousands, so 100 here or there, no big deal. However, when you open those electronic files, then you find that you are actually dealing with 391 files. And depending on which -- which kind of files those are, because they're all image files, it is altogether with other -- with other folder which is Rule 66 material, by the way, it's all together not more than 5.100 pages. So you know, it's not one afternoon, two afternoon or something like that, it is couple of days of work of quite a considerable part of the team. Beside, in the same -- by the same letter dated 16 March, the Prosecution is advising us that in addition they would send us material on DVD. Those consisting -- consisted of either audio or video files, and those are, as much as I checked, and I checked quite -- but not all, are mostly actually substitutes for translation on the language that the accused understands, however, not provided in the paper form. Rather, it is on audio and video. There is -- I will not go into -- into the details, but those DVDs, one of them again is again Rule 68. There are 16 audio files. The other ones are 66 -- Rule 66 with 27, 14, 14, 25, et cetera, et cetera. So in other words, the accused is obviously entitled to receive the material on the language he understands. We are aware of the problems, technical problems of the Prosecution that sometimes, but that is an exception, there should be exception, they are not able to provide a written translation. So instead they are supplying us with -- they are giving us a video or audio material. So you can imagine, Your Honour. The witness is interviewed by the Prosecution's investigators, usually full day, sometimes two days, sometimes three days. So instead having that material typed down on Croatian for my client and he can read it in couple of hours and I can read it in couple of hours, even so I would -- I'm reading the English one, English text, he would need exactly the same amount of time as it was needed for original interview. So if we do some mathematics, I would say that only for this particular case, only for those couple of videos and audio material, my client should stay in Zagreb or Scheveningen, it doesn't matter, for the next two or three months working every day eight hours only in order to hear what some witness said during the interview. Again, I will not complain if here or there because of error or omission we are all working with thousands and thousands and thousands of documents the Prosecution failed to produce a translation at the due time. So instead they will give me video. No problem. We'll be happy to accommodate. However, if that is the practice, and by the way this is not the first time but I will not elaborate any further because I have -- do not have all data with me, but this one I took, then our time is wasted. We cannot do what we have to do. I need my client in preparing, for example, pre-trial brief. He is has the information. He was there, not I. I know something, some details. I read some documents. I heard some witnesses, potential witnesses. I learned something about. But he was there, and I'm not ready to state the facts without having input from my client. Why? Because the Prosecution sees an opportunity here. Let's keep the client in the dark or at least delay him for a couple of months. So I'm not able to discuss -- now I'm coming to the point. I'm not able to discuss some of those witnesses some of those because the -- my client haven't yet read the translation, or I have of course alternative, first to spend one or two of my staff which is very poor and restricted, you know the policy of the registry, to translate for the client and then I can talk about him and see whether those witnesses are really important for me. And then I can tell you, Your Honour, I will have ten documents for that witness. I will need to cross him on that or that, and I believe it will be one hour or ten hours. So we are kept in the dark, Your Honour, as much as possible and as long as possible. And this is the clear example. The Prosecution is giving the one which my colleague Karnavas showed one hour earlier with audiotapes we received today, the one which you inform you which was given to us by Prosecution letter 16 March, et cetera, et cetera. So unfortunately we will see. I'm not talking on behalf of other colleagues. I have to wait and see which witness will actually come, what the witness will actually say or not, and what I got before that in order to go into the details. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As -- as far as what you have both said -- from what I understood after listening to Mr. Scott, the first witnesses to be called are some kind of a patchwork aimed at illustrating the entire case. Mr. Karnavas talked about a Hollywood production. Sometimes, you know, they are of very high quality, those Hollywood productions. So let's wait and see how that patchwork pans out. Normally it should be connected to the oral evidence of the case when the trial begins. So if I understand properly, in their presentation the Prosecution is going to articulate the reasoning of the entire case, its logics, and then we will have the illustration thereof through witnesses. Only after will they sort of stick to this logics with the witness -- witnesses coming. That's the way I understood things. Mr. Kovacic, you said it was differ to use electronic communication. I fully agree with you, and this is why you're here today. I realised the problem. I realised that Mr. Praljak was representing himself, did not have any lawyers, and he was receiving exhibits electronically. So he had a problem with documents that were not translated into his language. That was a real problem. To arrive at a solution we had to have lawyers appointed to him very quickly. That is how you came to be here, the two of you. It's true that some documents are in English when they are transmitted electronically. The idea is that lawyers know both English and B/C/S, and they are able to communicate with their respective clients. But what about the numerous video material? Indeed, some of it is not translated. Further to my request, I received the CD-ROMs and I started viewing them. I noticed that and lot of the reports had not been translated. Some had been. Some others had not. So I immediately wanted to know when the Prosecutor was planning to introduce this video material. There are two ways of going about it, the way we used in the Hadzihasanovic case and the usual way. In the Hadzihasanovic case we took several days to view the video material. Everybody saw them in court, the various excerpts, and then the lawyers could challenge the reliability of the video material and then we ruled on their admissibility. That's one possible technique. There is another one. Based on the witness list and the exhibit list, video material can be introduced. Let's take a simple case, Mostar. We have a lot of video footage, a great deal of video footage on Mostar. The Prosecution could call a witness from Mostar, put a few questions to that witness and straight away say, "I seek to introduce this video footage." It is broadcast, and the Prosecution continues questioning the witness. "Did you see this? Were you on the spot?" They seek to introduce that video evidence. But it all depends on the list that I requested of the Prosecution, but based on the witness we should have the documents as well. But even if you do not have this, even if you do not understand the language that is spoken to, do the same as I did, view the video material, listen, and you can use it later in cross-examination. Because when we are shown the video material, you will not have the translation in the language of the accused. It's quite likely. But you know that when there is a video footage that is broadcast it is being interpreted by our interpreters, so it can be heard by the accused in their mother tongue. Of course we've got an interview with Mr. Praljak for over an hour. He speaks in his own native tongue, so there will be no problem for him, but there are other excerpts where you have a Spanish comment because the TVE journalists. I may understand Spanish, you may not. See we will have to have translation into B/C/S and English of the commentary in Spanish. So with regard to video material, I do urge the Prosecution to carry out a thorough check reminding them that sometimes when you call -- when you start the video excerpt you have the impression that this concerned a certain time period and then you realise that it's much longer. There is something happening in the snow. And then you saw it's the middle of the summer but it's the same footage. Something must have happened there. See, nothing escapes me. You just need to know that. So the onus is on the Prosecution to determine how they will introduce the video material. You have two possibilities. You show the footage to everybody during one or several hearings, or you seek to introduce that material witness by witness. You will decide on the case-by-case basis. I've got nothing to say about it. Anyway, when the Defence will start their case, if they have video material they will decide on the way to proceed. The time has come for a break. We'll have a break and then we'll tackle a few more subjects. We won't be able to deal with all of them. We'll start again at ten to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed for the last hour. We're going to try and speed up. First of all, following the questions put by the Prosecution as to the scheduling of their witnesses, one fundamental issue has been raised but we'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. I would like to address the question of expert witnesses. For the time being, I have been provided with a chart and a list of ten expert witnesses. 19 says the military expert, the 27 is a financial expert, number 60 is a historical witness, Mr. Donia, for whom we've received a report. Number 74 is a handwriting expert, 157 is a historian, 185 is a military expert, 218 is a historical expert, 222 is a demographer, and 226 is a historical witness, and 233 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also we have three other 92 bis witnesses. We don't know in which category this witness fits. Is he viva voce or is he a 92 bis witness. Also we have two legal experts that come under the 92 bis witness list so we have several historical witnesses here. Is that necessary? Would one historical witness not be enough? Why do we have so many historical witnesses? Second point, we have and handwriting expert. If we have a handwriting expert, this means that you feel that some documents have been challenged. A handwriting expert will come along to say that this is Mr. Praljak's signature. This is Mr. Prlic's signature. But maybe none of this is challenged. So I don't know if whether it's really useful to call a handwriting expert unless you have a very clear idea about this which I'm not informed about. Now, as far as the military expert is concerned, I don't know what kind of witness this is. Is he going to talk about angles of shooting or firearms or snipers? I'm not quite sure. Firing angles. Also, we have a demographer. Is this a real issue? We know that in the various municipalities the ethnic composition was different. Is it useful to look into this in too more detail, particularly in the event that the Defence has no particular comments to make about this. Is it necessary to call a demographer? Now, let me turn to Mr. Donia's report now. We have all received this report. The first thing I'd like to say is that I would have liked to see footnotes on this report. I would have preferred the reference number to refer to -- not to the ERN numbers but your exhibit list numbers. It would have made my life easier. It makes it easier to follow because an ERN number is a lot more complicated to locate. For instance on page 40 in the footnote it is stipulated B/C/S 004498892. Would have been easier just to give us a number which is already on your list. So much for some of the comments I wanted to make. Theoretically, pursuant to Article 94 bis, the Defence reads the report and has one month to respond to it. So we do have a date problem here, because it takes a month for the report to be provided. If the report -- the report, of course, has to be handed over before the witness is called to testify. The Defence can perhaps tell us what kind of difficulties it come up against in a case like this. I have looked at this report. No major difficulty will arise, perhaps, but -- cross-examination might suffice, but I don't know what the position of the Prosecution and the Defence is. Now, as far as expert witnesses are concerned, could you shed some light on all of this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, as -- I don't have the numbers. Your Honour very -- very efficiently had the number of the witness and you were referring to -- I don't have those readily available to me in a prepared form. So just to avoid possibly saying something, could we go to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to Dr. Donia's report, if you -- if that's what you want to call it, I choose not to, it's not an expert report. The first thing I notice that it had some footnotes, more than the one than he had in the previous case where he didn't have any, and it's rather shocking and appalling for someone who is an academic or a supposed academic from a very good institution holding a Ph.D. in history over a period of time for which is not relevant to the indictment. I don't find this report to be a report. It covers some issues. I think the title of it says -- I can't recall exactly, but it -- it doesn't cover the entire period. It just covers some of the issues or some of the periods. There are some periods that are in this document that are not relevant to the issues at hand. At one of the 65 ter meetings, Mr. Scott said that he bet the Defence would be raising issues dating back to the 1500s. Well, and I made it clear that I had no intentions of going back that far or even further. I want to stick to the period of the indictment. 1991, 1994. Now, we can go back a few years, but I don't see the need to be going back into the Middle Ages or even before that. So we challenge that report or that document. I will be -- I'm willing to file something to say exactly what it is that I challenge. There are some things that I find troubling. Some of his conclusions. He makes sweeping generalisations and statements without making references, and then when he does make references, he's quoting newspapers in many instances. So how can a newspaper where you have during the period of a wartime or a turbulent period where newspapers are notoriously connected to one political party or one nation or another, how can you rely on that as authority upon which you're going to draw a conclusion as an academic from which then you're going to ask the Court to buy in to make a reasonable conclusion from. So we do challenge that report, and I don't think it should be admitted at all. Dr. Donia can come in here and he can defend himself. He can present whatever it is he wants to present. He's testified on numerous occasions on all sides, and he can do so, but that is not a report, Your Honour, and I might want to add, and I'm sure this will come out on the record during the trial, that he was a hired gun by the Prosecution. He was an employee of the Prosecution. He wasn't some expert that they hired independently, but he was an employee as an analyst, and now they turn him into an expert much as the other gentleman that was referred to by the Prosecutor. And we make that distinction between being someone who is being very partisan, very subjective, being very prosecutorial minded with the result -- and result-oriented versus an independent expert who may disagree with others on the way they view certain matters and they make certain analysis, but Dr. Donia and the other gentlemen are certainly not experts. They're Prosecution employees, former albeit, but nonetheless they're employees. And it's no different than having, sort of, one of the Prosecutors testifying over here in the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you all are on the same wavelength. I just 15 minutes left, so we have to save time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something not in relation to this but in relation to another very important matter that you raised and to which the Prosecution did not reply and that has to do with the footnote number of the Prosecutor's brief. I think that your suggestion concerning that number and definition of that number is very important for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed regarding footnotes both for the Prosecution brief and the expert report. The Prosecution now have a list of exhibits. Could they in their pre-trial brief adapt that idea to make references to the list and not to ERN numbers? It would be so much easier. It shouldn't be too complicated, especially given the resources you have at your disposal. It should be easy for you to do the work and convey to me a pre-trial brief that would give references to the exhibit list. As to your expert, be they paid by the OTP or not, you could ask them to do the work. Regarding this expert, I do not have his resume. I don't know who Mr. Donia is, in fact. The Defence will have to give me a reply by the 13th of April regarding this report. I can see that you want it not to be admitted and you want the witness to come to testify. We are still in private session -- oh, no, we're not in private session. Let's move back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in open session let me say that this hearing, this Status Conference is now coming to an end. The next Status Conference will be held on the 12th of April at 9.00 a.m., unless I'm mistaken, and like today we will have the entire morning to deal with issues that have not been dealt with residual issues. I hope Mrs. Carla Del Ponte will come and tell us how she intends addressing this case pursuant to the security resolution -- to the Resolution passed by the Security Council, because this is a matter of some substance. And then we shall address all the other questions. There are a number of items I was unable to address today like the tendering into evidence of some of the exhibits. We had planned for -- after the 12th of April to have a demonstration of the e-court system, but if we do not have enough time to do this, I will first of all deal with the Status Conference and the e-court system is something you could address at another time, some other time. When we did the demo, I asked to have a colour printer. I was told that there would -- a colour printer would be provided, and like in Hollywood, you will have documents that will be printed out in colour. And I also asked to have larger screens, and in an ideal case we would have had a screen like you have in movie theatres in order to show these videos. I was told that I would be provided with a screen, but I don't know how big and large the screen will be. So I don't know what the registry has done about this, but at any rate this -- they're making sure that this trial unfolds in the best way possible. So we shall reconvene again on the 12th of April. The Court stands adjourned.
